---
title: "How to read a page"
---

Every model page opens with one screen of panels: a drawing of the task, the task settings, the
parameters, the predicted responses, and the prediction across task settings. Move any control and
every panel follows. The dashed lines and outlines show the model at bmm's prior means, so a change is
always a comparison. Each slider covers the range bmm's default priors consider plausible.

Below the panels, every page has the same five parts.

1. **What the model says.** The model in a few sentences and its formula, with the parameters named
   as bmm names them.
2. **The task.** A drawing of the experimental trial the model is written for. Where the task has
   settings that enter the model (how many items, how many response candidates), the drawing follows
   the controls.
3. **Explore.** How to read the panels, and where the slider ranges come from.
4. **Across task settings.** Some models predict how responses change when the task changes while the
   parameters stay the same: more candidates, more items on the screen. Those pages show that
   prediction. Models whose likelihood has no such setting say so, which is worth knowing before an
   experiment is designed around one.
5. **In bmm.** The call that fits the model you are looking at, and the density call with the current
   values, ready to paste into R.

The curves are computed in your browser by small JavaScript copies of bmm's density functions. Each
copy is tested against values produced by bmm itself; the test and the fixtures are in the
[repository](https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/bmm-explorer/tree/main/tests/parity).
